name: OMK 2A Psych Exam 2 — Psychosis, Antipsychotics & Extrapyramidal Symptoms

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man is brought to the office by his mother because he has been telling relatives that a rival software company implanted receivers in his molars to capture his ideas before he can patent them. His mother states that this began in March and it is now August. He withdrew from his final semester of engineering school, quit his part-time job at a bicycle shop, and now leaves the apartment only to buy food. She says his speech has become hard to follow — "he starts on one thing and ends up somewhere else entirely." He reports hearing two voices that comment on what he is doing. He has never had a period of depressed mood, loss of interest, elevated mood, or decreased need for sleep. He takes no medications and has never used stimulants; urine toxicology screening is negative. Temperature is 36.8°C (98.2°F), pulse is 76/min, and blood pressure is 118/74 mm Hg. Physical and neurologic examinations show no abnormalities. Serum TSH, complete blood count, and comprehensive metabolic panel are within normal limits, and noncontrast CT of the head shows no abnormalities. On mental status examination, affect is flat, speech is tangential, and he has no insight into the belief about the receivers. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Do the arithmetic the stem hands you: March to August is 5 months, which lands squarely in the 1-to-6-month window for schizophreniform disorder. He meets psychosis criteria several times over (bizarre delusion, running-commentary auditory hallucinations, disorganized speech, flat affect as a negative symptom) and only one is required. The dramatic decoy is the severity — a failed semester, a lost job, near-total withdrawal, and a flat affect all feel like "real" schizophrenia, but functional decline is not the discriminator between these two; duration is, and he has not reached 6 months. Board pearl — brief psychotic, schizophreniform, and schizophrenia share identical symptom criteria and differ only on the clock: 1 day to 1 month, 1 to 6 months, and more than 6 months, so date arithmetic in the first sentence is never scenery.

wrongExplanations.0: Brief psychotic disorder requires at least 1 day but less than 1 month of symptoms. At 5 months he passed that ceiling four months ago.
wrongExplanations.2: Schizophrenia requires more than 6 months of continuous disturbance. He is at 5 months — if the mother had said February instead of March, this would be the answer, which is exactly why the month is stated twice.
wrongExplanations.3: Schizoaffective disorder requires a major mood episode concurrent with active psychosis. He explicitly has never had depressed mood, loss of interest, elevated mood, or decreased need for sleep, so there is no mood episode to concur with anything.
wrongExplanations.4: Delusional disorder requires a plausible, non-bizarre fixed delusion with otherwise preserved functioning and no prominent hallucinations. Implanted molar receivers is a bizarre delusion, he has running-commentary auditory hallucinations, and his functioning has collapsed.
wrongExplanations.5: Schizotypal personality disorder is a lifelong pattern of odd beliefs, magical thinking, and eccentric behavior without frank, fixed delusions or true hallucinations. His symptoms began at a datable point 5 months ago and include both.

questions.eli5: He truly believes there are radios in his teeth and he hears voices talking about him. Doctors put a stopwatch on this: under a month is one name, one to six months is another, and over six months is a third. He is at five months, so he gets the middle name.

questions.stem: A 54-year-old man is on hospital day 3 after open reduction and internal fixation of an ankle fracture. Overnight he began pointing at the wall and describing insects crawling across it, and he pulled out his intravenous line twice. His wife says he drinks a pint of vodka every evening and had his last drink on the morning of admission. She adds that he had two seizures during a detoxification admission 6 years ago. He has no personal or family history of a psychotic disorder and has never taken an antipsychotic medication. He is afebrile, HR 122, BP 168/98, RR 22. He is diaphoretic and coarsely tremulous, is oriented to person only, and his attention fluctuates over the course of the interview. Fingerstick glucose is 118 mg/dL, urine toxicology screening is negative, there are no focal neurologic deficits or meningismus, and CT of the head shows no abnormalities. What is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy?
questions.explanation: This is delirium tremens on day 3 off alcohol — the "downers in withdrawal" half of the substance-psychosis rule, where the psychosis belongs to the withdrawal state and not to a primary psychotic disorder. A long-acting benzodiazepine is the answer because it is the only listed agent that is cross-reactive at GABA-A, and its active metabolites smooth the taper and lower the chance of recurrent withdrawal or seizures. The buried clue is the pair of prior withdrawal seizures: that history makes seizure prevention the deciding constraint rather than an afterthought, and alcohol withdrawal is the single most lethal withdrawal syndrome precisely because of seizures and delirium tremens. Board pearl — the dramatic decoy here is the hallucination, which tempts an antipsychotic; treat the withdrawal and the hallucinations go with it.

wrongExplanations.1: Clonidine is an alpha-2 agonist that blunts the sympathetic surge of withdrawal and partially covers opioid and nicotine withdrawal, but it does not adequately prevent withdrawal seizures — which is exactly why it is never adequate monotherapy for CNS-depressant withdrawal, and exactly why his seizure history rules it out.
wrongExplanations.2: Haloperidol treats the surface complaint (the visual hallucinations) while leaving the GABA-A/NMDA rebound untouched, and it lowers the seizure threshold in a patient who has already had withdrawal seizures. He has no personal or family history of a psychotic disorder, so there is no primary psychosis for it to address.
wrongExplanations.3: Olanzapine has the same problem as haloperidol — it is a dopamine blocker aimed at a symptom rather than at the withdrawal physiology — and it adds sedation and metabolic burden without any seizure protection.
wrongExplanations.4: Phenytoin does not prevent alcohol withdrawal seizures, which are generated by acute GABA-A/NMDA rebound rather than by a chronic epileptogenic focus; benzodiazepines, not phenytoin, are the agents shown to prevent them.

questions.eli5: His body got used to alcohol every night, and three days without it left his brain running way too fast — shaky, sweaty, and seeing bugs that are not there. A long-acting sedative from the same family calms the brain back down and, most importantly, stops him from having a seizure.

questions.stem: A 21-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by campus police after he was found shouting at a parking-garage security camera, which he says has been transmitting his thoughts to a foreign government. His roommate reports 8 months of increasing isolation, a failed semester, and muttering to an unseen listener in their room. He takes no medications, urine toxicology screening is negative, and he has never used stimulants. Temperature is 37.0°C (98.6°F), pulse is 92/min, and blood pressure is 124/78 mm Hg; physical and neurologic examinations show no abnormalities. He is admitted and started on haloperidol 5 mg PO twice daily, and over the next 4 days he stops responding to the voice and no longer mentions the camera. The improvement in this patient's symptoms is most directly attributable to dopamine blockade in which of the following pathways?
questions.explanation: The mesolimbic tract governs motivation and reward and is overactive in psychosis; excess dopamine here drives the positive symptoms — hallucinations, delusions, disorganized speech and behavior. Blocking D2 receptors in this tract → reduced mesolimbic dopamine signaling → resolution of the voice and the camera belief. That is the therapeutic effect, and it is the only one of the four tracts where blockade is wanted. Board pearl — one receptor, four pathways, four different outcomes: block the mesolimbic tract and psychosis improves, and the other three blocks are your side-effect chapters.

wrongExplanations.0: The mesocortical tract handles cognition and motivation and is already underactive in psychosis. Blocking dopamine there worsens or fails to help negative and cognitive symptoms — it produces a problem rather than the benefit described.
wrongExplanations.1: The nigrostriatal tract runs the extrapyramidal motor system. Blockade there tips the striatal acetylcholine:dopamine balance toward relative cholinergic excess and produces EPS, not resolution of hallucinations.
wrongExplanations.3: The tuberoinfundibular tract is where dopamine tonically inhibits prolactin release. Blockade there disinhibits prolactin and produces galactorrhea, amenorrhea, and gynecomastia, with no effect on psychotic symptoms.

questions.eli5: There are four dopamine highways in the brain. The medicine puts up a roadblock on all of them, but only one of those roadblocks is the one you actually wanted — the one that quiets the voices and the false beliefs.

questions.stem: Forty-eight hours after the first dose of haloperidol described in the preceding vignette, the same 21-year-old man's neck twists involuntarily to the left and his eyes deviate upward and remain fixed there. He is frightened and his speech is slurred. He is afebrile; pulse is 104/min and blood pressure is 130/82 mm Hg. Muscle tone is increased in the neck and jaw only; there is no generalized rigidity, no diaphoresis, and deep tendon reflexes are 2+ throughout with no clonus. He denies any subjective urge to move and is able to sit still in the chair. What is the most appropriate initial treatment for these motor symptoms?
questions.explanation: Sudden, sustained muscle contraction — here torticollis plus oculogyric crisis — within hours to days of a high-potency typical is an acute dystonic reaction, and young men on first exposure are the classic highest-risk group. D2 blockade in the nigrostriatal tract → relative cholinergic excess in the striatum → sustained contraction, so the fix is an anticholinergic given by a route that works in minutes. Benztropine 2 mg IM is that answer, and the relief is often dramatic. Board pearl — the whole option set here is correct drugs at wrong routes or for wrong EPS subtypes: in acute dystonia, the route is as much of the answer as the molecule, because dysarthria and jaw involvement can progress to laryngeal spasm.

wrongExplanations.0: Amantadine is a dopamine agonist used for pseudoparkinsonism, not for acute dystonia, and an oral agent takes far too long for a reaction that is already involving his jaw and speech.
wrongExplanations.1: Diphenhydramine is the right pharmacologic idea — it is the antihistamine alternative to benztropine for dystonia — but by mouth it is too slow, and 25 mg PO will not abort an oculogyric crisis in progress.
wrongExplanations.2: Stopping the antipsychotic does nothing for the contraction already occurring and leaves an acutely distressed patient with jaw and speech involvement untreated. Stopping the drug is the first step for tardive dyskinesia and for neuroleptic malignant syndrome, not for acute dystonia — and he is afebrile with no generalized rigidity, so this is neither.
wrongExplanations.4: Propranolol is first-line for akathisia. He explicitly denies any urge to move and can sit still, which is the negative that removes akathisia from consideration.
wrongExplanations.5: Trihexyphenidyl is an appropriate anticholinergic for drug-induced parkinsonism and can be used chronically, but the oral route is too slow for an acute dystonic reaction.

questions.eli5: His neck locked to one side and his eyes rolled up and stuck there two days after starting the new medicine. A shot of an anticholinergic in the muscle unlocks it within minutes — a pill would take too long while his jaw and voice are already involved.

questions.stem: The dystonic reaction described above resolves within 20 minutes. Three weeks later the same patient, now maintained on haloperidol 5 mg PO twice daily with continued improvement in his delusions, tells the nurse that he feels "like my legs have to go somewhere." He is observed rocking from foot to foot at the medication window and cannot remain seated through a 20-minute group session; he stands and paces four times. He denies depressed mood, denies worry about any specific thing, and denies any return of the belief about the camera. He is afebrile; pulse is 88/min and blood pressure is 122/76 mm Hg. There is no tremor at rest, no cogwheel rigidity, and no orofacial or lingual movement. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
choices: A. Add benztropine 1 mg PO twice daily
B. Add propranolol 20 mg PO three times daily
C. Increase haloperidol to 10 mg PO twice daily
questions.explanation: Subjective inner restlessness plus visible inability to sit still, arriving days to weeks into a high-potency typical, is akathisia, and propranolol is classically first-line; benzodiazepines are the usual second option. The trap is that akathisia is the one EPS syndrome that does not respond well to the anticholinergic reflex that works for dystonia and pseudoparkinsonism — reaching for benztropine here is the single most common wrong move. His stated negatives do real work: no depressed mood and no focused worry separate akathisia from agitation and anxiety, and no tremor, rigidity, or orofacial movement separate it from pseudoparkinsonism and tardive dyskinesia. Board pearl — akathisia is dose-related, so escalating the antipsychotic to "cover the restlessness" makes the very side effect you are treating worse.

wrongExplanations.0: Benztropine is the classic choice for acute dystonia and drug-induced parkinsonism, but it is a distinctly less reliable treatment for akathisia specifically than a beta-blocker — and he has neither tremor nor rigidity for it to address.
wrongExplanations.2: Akathisia is a dose-related consequence of striatal D2 occupancy climbing past the roughly 78-80% EPS threshold. Doubling the dose pushes occupancy higher and predictably worsens the restlessness, and his delusions are already improving, so there is no efficacy reason to escalate.
wrongExplanations.3: This is the sophisticated-sounding switch that the data do not support: the aripiprazole-family partial agonists carry some of the highest reported akathisia rates of any antipsychotics, so switching to one to treat akathisia risks trading sideways at best.
wrongExplanations.4: Chlorpromazine is a low-potency typical with less EPS, but switching agents abandons a medication that is working on his psychosis to treat a side effect that has a simple, effective, first-line drug — and it buys a heavy anticholinergic, sedating, alpha-blocking burden instead.

questions.eli5: He is not anxious and he is not sad — his body just will not let him sit down. That specific side effect is treated with a beta-blocker, not with the anticholinergic that fixed his neck three weeks ago, and definitely not by raising the dose that caused it.

questions.stem: A 44-year-old woman with schizophrenia is being switched to a different antipsychotic because of persistent auditory hallucinations on her current agent. She has had three episodes of syncope in the past year, two of them while walking. She takes furosemide for lower-extremity edema. She is afebrile, HR 68, BP 118/72, RR 14. Serum K+ is 3.2 mEq/L and Mg2+ is 1.6 mg/dL. ECG shows sinus rhythm with a QTc interval of 486 ms. Her BMI is 23 kg/m2, fasting glucose is 88 mg/dL, and hemoglobin A1c is 5.2%. She has never had agranulocytosis or any drug-induced movement disorder, and she is not pregnant. What medication should be avoided by the prescriber in this case?
questions.explanation: Every option on this list would treat her psychosis, so the psychiatric picture is scenery and the decision is made entirely by the cardiac data. Ziprasidone carries the strongest QT-prolongation signal among the atypical antipsychotics, and she arrives with a QTc of 486 ms plus a loop diuretic driving hypokalemia and hypomagnesemia — three additive risks for torsades in a woman already having syncopal episodes. Board pearl — the decoy is that ziprasidone is one of the metabolically cleanest atypicals, so a reader ranking these agents by weight gain picks it as the safe choice; her normal BMI, glucose, and A1c are the planted negatives that make metabolic risk irrelevant here and force the QT axis instead.

wrongExplanations.0: Aripiprazole sits at the lowest-risk end of the QT-prolongation table along with lurasidone, and it is also lowest for metabolic burden and prolactin elevation. There is nothing in this stem that argues against it.
wrongExplanations.1: Clozapine's disqualifying histories are agranulocytosis and its monitoring burden, and the stem explicitly states she has never had agranulocytosis. Its risks are hematologic, seizure-related, and cardiac in the myocarditis sense, not QT interval prolongation.
wrongExplanations.2: Lurasidone shares the lowest-QT slot with aripiprazole and carries low metabolic risk, making it one of the more reasonable choices for exactly this patient rather than the one to avoid.
wrongExplanations.3: Olanzapine's liability is metabolic — the highest weight gain and type 2 diabetes risk of the class alongside clozapine. Her BMI of 23 kg/m2, fasting glucose of 88 mg/dL, and A1c of 5.2% are the explicit negatives that neutralize that concern.
wrongExplanations.4: Risperidone's signature problems are frequent hyperprolactinemia and, as a "-done," more EPS than the "-pines." The stem states she has never had a drug-induced movement disorder and she is not pregnant, and neither issue involves the QT interval.

questions.eli5: All six of these medicines would help her hear fewer voices, so the choice comes down to her heart tracing, which already shows a long reset time. One of the six stretches that reset even longer, and her water pill has dropped her body salts, which makes it riskier still.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman comes to the office because of a 3-month history of absent menstrual periods and a milky discharge from both nipples that she first noticed on her shirt. She began an antipsychotic 5 months ago for schizophrenia, and her auditory hallucinations have resolved completely. Her BMI is 22 kg/m2, unchanged from before she started the medication. She takes no other prescription medications, herbal products, or over-the-counter agents, and she has had no head trauma. Urine pregnancy test is negative, serum TSH is 1.8 μU/mL, and visual fields are full to confrontation. Serum prolactin is 96 ng/mL. She has had no tremor, rigidity, or restlessness. Which of the following antipsychotics is she most likely taking?
questions.explanation: Work backward from the effect. Dopamine tonically inhibits prolactin release through the tuberoinfundibular tract, so D2 blockade there → disinhibited prolactin → galactorrhea, amenorrhea, and gynecomastia. Among the atypicals, risperidone and its active metabolite paliperidone sit at the top of the prolactin-elevation table, and risperidone is the agent classically described as causing frequent hyperprolactinemia. The stated negatives are load-bearing and each closes a competing explanation: a negative pregnancy test, a normal TSH, and full visual fields eliminate pregnancy, hypothyroidism, and a chiasm-compressing prolactinoma. Board pearl — the unchanged BMI is the quiet detail that steers you away from the "-pines": the famous antipsychotic side effect is weight gain, and its absence here is what makes prolactin the axis in play.

wrongExplanations.0: Aripiprazole sits at the lowest-risk end of the prolactin table — as a D2 partial agonist it stabilizes rather than fully blocks dopamine tone, so it is the agent least likely to produce hyperprolactinemia, and it is often used to reverse it.
wrongExplanations.1: Clozapine has essentially no prolactin elevation, which is one of its notable "unique lack of side effects" alongside its absence of EPS and tardive dyskinesia. Its problems are agranulocytosis, seizures, sialorrhea, myocarditis, and heavy metabolic burden.
wrongExplanations.2: Olanzapine is a "-pine" whose signature adverse effects are weight gain, sedation, and metabolic syndrome. Her BMI is explicitly unchanged at 22 kg/m2, and olanzapine is not a leading cause of hyperprolactinemia.
wrongExplanations.3: Quetiapine has essentially no prolactin elevation. Its recognizable liabilities are sedation from H1 antagonism, orthostatic hypotension, and metabolic burden.

questions.eli5: Dopamine normally acts like a lid on the hormone that makes breast milk. Her medicine blocks dopamine, the lid comes off, milk shows up and her periods stop — and one medicine in this list is far more likely than the others to do that.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man with schizophrenia has taken olanzapine 20 mg PO daily for 2 years, with complete resolution of his auditory hallucinations and persecutory beliefs and no missed doses documented on pharmacy refill records. He has gained 38 lb (17 kg) during that period, and his BMI has risen from 26 to 33 kg/m2. Blood pressure is 128/80 mm Hg. Fasting serum glucose is 152 mg/dL, hemoglobin A1c is 7.9%, and serum triglycerides are 310 mg/dL; both glucose and A1c were normal before he started the medication. ECG shows a QTc interval of 402 ms. He has had no extrapyramidal symptoms, no galactorrhea, and no sedation that interferes with his work. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
choices: A. Continue olanzapine and add metformin
questions.explanation: He has developed frank type 2 diabetes and dyslipidemia on the antipsychotic that, with clozapine, anchors the highest-risk end of the metabolic table. When diabetes or substantial weight gain emerges on an antipsychotic, consensus guidance is to move the patient to an agent at the low-risk end rather than to layer a second chronic medication on top of the cause — and aripiprazole shows up on the "lowest risk" side of nearly every side-effect row, with the cleanest metabolic profile of the group. Board pearl — diabetes risk in psychiatric patients already runs 2 to 4 times the general-population baseline before any drug is added, and ziprasidone is the other guideline-named low-metabolic switch, though its QT signal has to be checked first.

wrongExplanations.0: Adding metformin treats the consequence while the drug generating it continues at full dose. It is a defensible move when no acceptable alternative antipsychotic exists, but here several low-metabolic-risk agents are available, so it is second-best.
wrongExplanations.2: Clozapine sits beside olanzapine at the highest-risk end of the metabolic table and adds agranulocytosis, seizure, sialorrhea, and myocarditis risk. It is also reserved for treatment-resistant disease, and his psychosis is in full remission — this switch worsens the exact problem being solved.
wrongExplanations.3: Quetiapine is a "-pine" and sits in the middle-to-upper band for weight gain, glucose, and lipids, along with prominent sedation. Moving from one metabolically burdensome agent to another does not resolve a new A1c of 7.9%.
wrongExplanations.4: Risperidone carries less metabolic burden than olanzapine but is not at the low-risk end, and it brings frequent hyperprolactinemia and more EPS as a "-done." Aripiprazole is the cleaner metabolic landing spot.

questions.eli5: The medicine cleared his voices but also gave him diabetes and almost 40 extra pounds. Rather than adding a diabetes pill on top and leaving the cause running, switch him to the antipsychotic that is gentlest on weight and blood sugar.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old man with schizophrenia has completed an 8-week trial of risperidone at 6 mg PO daily and a 10-week trial of olanzapine at 20 mg PO daily, each at an adequate dose with adherence confirmed by pill counts and refill records. He continues to hear a voice telling him to step into traffic, and he has made two suicide attempts in the past 14 months, one of which required intubation. He has had no extrapyramidal symptoms. His BMI is 24 kg/m2, fasting glucose is 90 mg/dL, ECG shows a QTc interval of 410 ms, absolute neutrophil count is 4,800/mm3, aminotransferases are within normal limits, and serum creatinine is 0.9 mg/dL. His psychiatrist plans to start the antipsychotic with the strongest evidence for this specific situation. Which of the following must be monitored on a mandatory scheduled basis once that medication is started?
questions.explanation: Two inferential steps, and the drug is never named. Step one: two adequate-dose, adequate-duration trials with documented adherence and persistent symptoms defines treatment-resistant schizophrenia, and recurrent suicidal behavior points the same direction — clozapine is both the superior agent for treatment-resistant disease and the only antipsychotic FDA-approved to reduce recurrent suicidal behavior in schizophrenia and schizoaffective disorder. Step two: clozapine's unique risk is agranulocytosis in roughly 1 to 2% of patients, so mandatory ANC/WBC monitoring under a REMS program is the price of prescribing it, running weekly at first and stretching out with continued normal counts. Board pearl — the action thresholds escalate from increased monitoring frequency, to interrupting therapy with daily counts, to permanent discontinuation with no rechallenge once severe neutropenia occurs.

wrongExplanations.0: Scheduled QTc surveillance is the monitoring burden associated with ziprasidone and thioridazine. His QTc is already normal at 410 ms, and QT is not what makes the agent indicated here uniquely restricted.
wrongExplanations.1: Serial aminotransferases are the monitoring signature of valproate's fatal hepatotoxicity risk, not of any antipsychotic, and his liver enzymes are already normal.
wrongExplanations.3: Serial creatinine and BUN belong to lithium, which is renally cleared and reabsorbed at the proximal tubule. His creatinine of 0.9 mg/dL is normal and the agent being started is an antipsychotic.
wrongExplanations.4: Prolactin rises with risperidone and paliperidone through tuberoinfundibular D2 blockade, but it is checked when symptoms of hyperprolactinemia appear rather than as mandatory scheduled surveillance — and the drug indicated here causes essentially no prolactin elevation.

questions.eli5: He has already failed two good medicine trials and keeps hearing a voice telling him to hurt himself, so there is really only one medicine left worth starting. That medicine can wipe out the white blood cells that fight infection, so his blood count has to be checked on a strict schedule.

questions.stem: A 46-year-old man with treatment-resistant schizophrenia maintained on clozapine 500 mg PO daily has been on a non-smoking inpatient medical unit for 6 days for cellulitis of the leg. Before admission he smoked 2 packs of cigarettes daily. On day 6 he is difficult to arouse, is drooling onto his gown, and has a witnessed generalized tonic-clonic seizure lasting 45 seconds. He is afebrile, HR 104, BP 108/66, RR 14. There is no rigidity, no diaphoresis, and deep tendon reflexes are 2+ throughout with no clonus. WBC is 7,200/mm3 with an absolute neutrophil count of 4,100/mm3, serum troponin is undetectable, and ECG shows sinus tachycardia without ST-segment changes. Serum sodium is 139 mEq/L, glucose is 96 mg/dL, and CT of the head shows no abnormalities. He drinks no alcohol and has been started on no other new medication. His serum clozapine concentration is markedly higher than his outpatient baseline. What is the underlying cause of his current condition?
choices: D. Loss of CYP1A2 induction after smoking cessation
questions.explanation: The hydrocarbons in cigarette smoke — not the nicotine — are CYP1A2 inducers, and clozapine and olanzapine are the two antipsychotics that are CYP1A2 substrates. Six smoke-free days removed that induction → CYP1A2 activity fell → clozapine metabolism slowed → serum levels climbed, reportedly by about 50% → sedation, sialorrhea, and a dose-related seizure at an unchanged prescribed dose. This is the mirror image of the more familiar version, in which a stabilized patient resumes smoking after discharge and relapses despite perfect adherence. Board pearl — inducers risk efficacy loss and inhibitors risk toxicity, and roughly 95% of patients with psychotic disorders smoke, so both directions of this interaction are routine ward events rather than trivia.

wrongExplanations.0: Agranulocytosis is clozapine's unique 1 to 2% hematologic risk, but his WBC is 7,200/mm3 with an ANC of 4,100/mm3 and he is afebrile — the counts are the explicit negative that closes this option.
wrongExplanations.1: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome requires rigidity, hyperthermia, and diaphoresis after antipsychotic dosing. He is afebrile, has no rigidity, and is not diaphoretic — all three legs of the triad are absent.
wrongExplanations.2: Alcohol withdrawal is a genuine cause of seizure on hospital day 6 in a newly abstinent patient, which is why it belongs in the option set — but he drinks no alcohol, and his tremor-free, non-diaphoretic, normotensive presentation lacks the autonomic hyperactivity of withdrawal.
wrongExplanations.4: Clozapine myocarditis classically appears within the first weeks of therapy with chest pain, dyspnea, tachycardia, and elevated cardiac markers. He is 6 days into an admission on long-standing therapy with an undetectable troponin and a bland ECG.

questions.eli5: Cigarette smoke speeds up the liver enzyme that clears his medicine. Six days in a hospital where he could not smoke slowed that enzyme back down, so the medicine piled up until he was drowsy, drooling, and had a seizure — without anyone changing his dose.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old woman has taken haloperidol for 9 years for schizophrenia, and her psychotic symptoms have been in remission for the past 6 years. At her annual visit her daughter points out that for the past 8 months her mother has been continuously chewing, smacking her lips, and pushing her tongue against the inside of her cheek, even while sitting quietly watching television. The movements briefly stop when she is asked to open her mouth and resume when her attention shifts. She is afebrile, has no tremor at rest, no cogwheel rigidity, no sustained muscle contraction, and denies any subjective urge to move. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial step in management?
choices: A. Add amantadine 100 mg PO twice daily
B. Add benztropine 1 mg PO twice daily
C. Reduce the haloperidol dose and switch to an atypical agent
D. Add propranolol 20 mg PO three times daily
E. Increase the haloperidol dose and reassess in 8 weeks
questions.explanation: Involuntary, repetitive orofacial movements — chewing, lip-smacking, tongue protrusion — appearing after years of antipsychotic exposure are tardive dyskinesia, the chronic member of the EPS family. It is the one EPS syndrome whose initial management is to withdraw or reduce the offending agent and switch to an atypical, with a VMAT2 inhibitor considered if that is not enough. Board pearl — anticholinergics are the reflex answer for dystonia and pseudoparkinsonism, but they do not help tardive dyskinesia and can worsen it, because TD is not driven by the same relative-cholinergic-excess mechanism; TD is often irreversible, which is why prevention and early dose reduction matter more than any rescue drug.

wrongExplanations.0: Amantadine is used for pseudoparkinsonism, and she has neither the resting tremor, the cogwheel rigidity, nor the bradykinesia that syndrome requires — those negatives are stated explicitly.
wrongExplanations.1: Benztropine is the classic answer for acute dystonia and drug-induced parkinsonism, and it is the trap here. Anticholinergics do not improve tardive dyskinesia and may make it worse, since TD is not generated by relative cholinergic excess.
wrongExplanations.3: Propranolol is first-line for akathisia, which requires subjective restlessness and an urge to move. She explicitly denies any urge to move and sits quietly through television.
wrongExplanations.4: Raising the dose transiently suppresses the movements by increasing D2 blockade, which makes it seductive, but it deepens the underlying receptor supersensitivity and worsens the long-term course — the exact opposite of the correct direction.

questions.eli5: After nine years on the same medicine her mouth started chewing and smacking on its own, even when she is just watching TV. The fix is to slowly lower or change the medicine that caused it — the anticholinergic pill that helps other movement side effects does not help this one.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with schizophrenia was started on risperidone 4 mg PO daily 9 days ago. His wife says he now shuffles when he walks, his face "has gone blank," and his hands shake when they rest in his lap. He is afebrile, HR 76, BP 126/80, RR 14. Examination shows cogwheel rigidity at both wrists, bradykinesia, decreased arm swing, and a 4-Hz resting tremor. There is no sustained muscle contraction of the neck or eyes, no diaphoresis, and no orofacial or lingual movement; he denies any subjective urge to move and answers questions promptly, and his limbs do not remain in positions into which the examiner places them. Serum creatine kinase is 110 U/L. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Bradykinesia, cogwheel rigidity, resting tremor, and masked facies appearing within days to weeks of a new antipsychotic is drug-induced pseudoparkinsonism — nigrostriatal D2 blockade producing a relative dopamine deficiency that reaches the same final common pathway as idiopathic Parkinson disease. Risperidone is a "-done," the atypical subgroup that behaves like a watered-down typical and potentiates EPS more than the "-pines," so even a modest 4 mg dose can do this. Board pearl — this stem is built as a rule-out exercise: every negative in it eliminates exactly one option on the list, which is how a seven-option movement-disorder set is meant to be worked.

wrongExplanations.0: An acute dystonic reaction is a sudden, sustained muscle contraction such as torticollis or oculogyric crisis, arriving within hours to days. The stem states there is no sustained muscle contraction of the neck or eyes.
wrongExplanations.1: Akathisia is defined by subjective motor restlessness — the patient cannot sit still and feels compelled to move. He explicitly denies any urge to move.
wrongExplanations.2: Catatonia would show features such as waxy flexibility, in which limbs remain where the examiner places them, along with mutism or marked response latency. His limbs do not hold imposed postures and he answers questions promptly.
wrongExplanations.3: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome requires hyperthermia, diaphoresis, and lead-pipe rigidity with a markedly elevated creatine kinase. He is afebrile, is not diaphoretic, has cogwheel rather than lead-pipe tone, and his CK is 110 U/L.
wrongExplanations.5: Restless legs syndrome is a nocturnal urge to move the legs relieved by movement, not a daytime picture of rigidity, bradykinesia, and resting tremor — and he denies any urge to move at all.
wrongExplanations.6: Tardive dyskinesia is the chronic EPS syndrome, developing over months to years and presenting with choreoathetoid orofacial movements. He is 9 days into treatment with no orofacial or lingual movement.

questions.eli5: Nine days into a new medicine he walks stiffly, his face stopped moving, and his hands shake when they are just sitting still. That combination looks exactly like Parkinson disease, but the medicine caused it — which is why it gets the "pseudo" name.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man was brought to the emergency department 2 days ago by police for agitation and has received five doses of intramuscular haloperidol since arrival, the most recent 6 hours ago. He is now barely responsive to voice. Temperature is 40.1°C (104.2°F), pulse is 132/min, respirations are 24/min, and blood pressure is 158/94 mm Hg. He is diaphoretic, and his limbs resist passive movement uniformly through the full range with a lead-pipe quality. Deep tendon reflexes are 1+ throughout with no clonus and no tremor. Serum creatine kinase is 18,400 U/L and WBC is 16,200/mm3; urine is dark with a dipstick positive for blood but no red cells on microscopy. He has received no serotonergic medication and no inhaled anesthetic, and urine toxicology screening is negative. What is the most appropriate initial step in management?
questions.explanation: Rigidity, hyperthermia, and diaphoresis after repeated antipsychotic dosing is neuroleptic malignant syndrome, and the rhabdomyolysis picture — CK of 18,400 U/L with heme-positive urine containing no red cells — confirms the severity. The first and most essential step is to discontinue the causative dopamine blocker; supportive care with cooling and intravenous fluids follows, and dantrolene or bromocriptine are added in severe cases after the offending agent is stopped. The sequencing is the whole point: giving an antidote while the drug driving the syndrome is still being administered treats around the cause. Board pearl — 1+ reflexes with no clonus and a 2-day course are the negatives that separate NMS from serotonin syndrome, which runs the opposite way with hyperreflexia, clonus, and onset within hours.

wrongExplanations.1: Benztropine treats acute dystonia and drug-induced parkinsonism. His rigidity is generalized and lead-pipe with hyperthermia and rhabdomyolysis, which is not a dystonic reaction, and an anticholinergic also impairs sweating and heat dissipation in a patient at 40.1°C.
wrongExplanations.2: Bromocriptine is a dopamine agonist used to restore the dopaminergic tone lost to the antipsychotic, and it is a legitimate part of NMS management — but it is added in severe cases after the offending agent is stopped, not instead of stopping it.
wrongExplanations.3: Cyproheptadine is the 5-HT2 antagonist used for serotonin syndrome, which requires hyperreflexia and clonus. His reflexes are 1+ with no clonus, and the stem states he has received no serotonergic medication.
wrongExplanations.4: Dantrolene blocks calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum and is genuinely useful for the rigidity and heat generation of severe NMS — but it is a supportive measure layered on top of stopping the antipsychotic, which remains the first and most essential step.
wrongExplanations.5: Switching to a lower-potency typical still blocks dopamine and will not resolve an episode that is being driven by dopamine blockade. Any antipsychotic continued during active NMS perpetuates the syndrome.

questions.eli5: Two days of repeated shots of an antipsychotic left him burning hot, stiff as a board, and sweating, with muscle breaking down into his urine. Before any antidote, you stop giving the drug that is causing it.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by police after he was found pacing in the middle of an intersection, shouting that surveillance drones were tracking him. In the department he paces the hallway, clenches his fists, leans into the faces of staff members, and shouts obscenities at a nurse. Verbal de-escalation, an offer of food, and an offer of a quiet room have all failed. He has refused all oral medication, including an orally disintegrating tablet, and no intravenous access has been established. He is afebrile, HR 118, BP 146/88, RR 20. He is not known to this hospital, no medical records are available, and no medication history is obtainable from him or from the officers. What is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy?
choices: C. Diphenhydramine 50 mg, haloperidol 5 mg, and lorazepam 2 mg IM
D. Olanzapine 10 mg orally disintegrating tablet, repeated once
F. Diphenhydramine 50 mg and benztropine 1 mg IM
questions.explanation: This is the classic acute-agitation cocktail known as the B-52: Benadryl 50 mg, Haldol 5 mg, and Ativan 2 mg given intramuscularly as needed. Each component earns its place — haloperidol targets the psychosis driving the behavior, lorazepam provides rapid sedation, and diphenhydramine covers the acute dystonic reaction that a first dose of a high-potency typical can produce in exactly this demographic. The buried constraint is the route: he has refused every oral form including a dissolving tablet and has no intravenous access, so intramuscular administration is the only workable option, and that single sentence eliminates four of the six choices. Board pearl — the escalating warning signs that justify this intervention are behavioral as much as verbal: inability to sit still, fierce eye contact, clenched fists, and tensed jaw.

wrongExplanations.0: Chlorpromazine is a sedating low-potency typical that would blunt agitation, but it is offered by mouth and he has refused all oral medication. It also brings a heavy alpha-1 blocking burden and orthostatic hypotension in an undifferentiated patient with no medical history available.
wrongExplanations.1: Lorazepam alone is a reasonable sedative but is offered here by mouth, which he has refused, and monotherapy leaves the psychotic drive behind the behavior untreated.
wrongExplanations.3: An orally disintegrating olanzapine tablet is a genuinely good option for a cooperative agitated patient, which is why it is in the set — the stem specifically states he has refused oral medication including an orally disintegrating tablet.
wrongExplanations.4: Propranolol is first-line for akathisia, not for acute agitation, and it is oral. Nothing in this presentation suggests medication-induced restlessness; he has no known medication history at all.
wrongExplanations.5: Diphenhydramine plus benztropine is an intramuscular combination, so route is not the problem — but it is two anticholinergic agents with no antipsychotic and no benzodiazepine, so it treats a dystonic reaction he does not have while leaving the agitation entirely uncovered.

questions.eli5: He is too worked up to take anything by mouth and has no IV, so the medicine has to go in as a shot in the muscle. The standard shot mixes three drugs: one to calm the psychosis, one to settle him down, and one to prevent a muscle-locking side effect from the first.

questions.stem: An adult with schizophrenia who takes no antipsychotic medication at all has an approximate relapse rate of which of the following at 1 year?
questions.explanation: The unmedicated relapse figures are roughly 70% at 1 year and 90% at 2 years. Those numbers exist to be compared against the treated ones: approximately 20% per year on an oral antipsychotic, and approximately 5% per year on a long-acting injectable. Board pearl — the whole ladder is worth memorizing as one string, because it is the quantitative argument for long-acting injectables in a patient whose relapses track with missed doses, and it is far more persuasive to a patient than any qualitative statement about adherence.

wrongExplanations.0: Approximately 5% per year is the relapse rate on a long-acting injectable antipsychotic — the best figure on the ladder, and the reason LAIs are favored in patients with adherence-driven relapse.
wrongExplanations.1: Approximately 20% per year is the relapse rate for a patient taking an oral antipsychotic, which is roughly four times the LAI rate and still far better than no treatment.
wrongExplanations.2: 40% does not correspond to any figure in this set; it is the plausible-sounding midpoint a reader picks when hedging between the treated and untreated numbers.
wrongExplanations.4: Approximately 90% is the unmedicated relapse rate at 2 years rather than at 1 year — the closest near-miss on the list, separated from the answer only by the time frame in the question.

questions.eli5: If someone with schizophrenia takes nothing at all, about seven out of ten get sick again within a year. Taking a daily pill drops that to about two in ten, and a long-acting shot drops it to about one in twenty.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old man with schizophrenia is admitted for the third time in 18 months. Each admission has followed the same course: he stops taking oral risperidone 4 mg PO daily within 3 to 5 weeks of discharge, becomes convinced that his upstairs neighbor is pumping gas through the heating vents, and stops sleeping. Each time, his symptoms remit fully within 2 weeks of restarting the same dose of the same medication. He has never had extrapyramidal symptoms, akathisia, galactorrhea, or weight gain on risperidone, and he says he simply forgets doses when his work schedule changes. His BMI is 24 kg/m2, fasting glucose is 92 mg/dL, absolute neutrophil count is 5,100/mm3, and ECG shows a QTc interval of 408 ms. He states that he is willing to accept whatever treatment his physician recommends. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
choices: A. Add benztropine 1 mg PO twice daily
B. Increase the oral risperidone dose to 6 mg PO daily
questions.explanation: The buried clue is that he remits fully within 2 weeks every time the same dose of the same drug is restarted — the medication works, so this is an adherence problem, not a treatment-resistance problem. That single sentence redirects the entire question toward delivery rather than pharmacology, and the long-acting injectable is the intervention built for it: annual relapse rates run about 20% on oral therapy versus roughly 5% on an LAI. Paliperidone is risperidone's active metabolite, so he stays on the molecule already proven to work for him and already proven tolerable. Board pearl — the trap is that three hospitalizations in 18 months sounds like treatment resistance, but resistance requires failed adequate trials of two agents, and a drug that is not taken has never been given an adequate trial.

wrongExplanations.0: Benztropine treats acute dystonia and drug-induced parkinsonism. He has explicitly never had extrapyramidal symptoms, so there is nothing for it to prevent or treat, and it does not address why he relapses.
wrongExplanations.1: Raising the dose of a medication he is not taking changes nothing about the interval between discharge and discontinuation, and it adds EPS and prolactin risk to a regimen he currently tolerates well.
wrongExplanations.2: Psychosocial rehabilitation is the right answer for the patient whose symptoms are controlled and who is adherent but socially non-functioning. His symptoms are not controlled between admissions, and the immediate failure point is a missed dose rather than a functional deficit.
wrongExplanations.3: Clozapine is reserved for treatment-resistant disease, which requires failed trials of two agents at adequate dose and duration. He has never failed a trial — he has interrupted one three times — and clozapine adds agranulocytosis monitoring, seizure risk, and heavy metabolic burden for no gain here.
wrongExplanations.4: Switching to olanzapine abandons an agent he tolerates well and responds to, adds the highest-tier metabolic risk, and still relies on him remembering a daily oral dose — the exact step that keeps failing.

questions.eli5: The medicine works every single time he takes it — he just forgets it a few weeks after going home. So the answer is not a stronger or fancier medicine, it is the same medicine given as a long-acting shot he cannot forget.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man is started on chlorpromazine. Three days later he becomes lightheaded each time he stands, and his blood pressure falls from 132/80 mm Hg supine to 98/62 mm Hg after 2 minutes of standing. Blockade of which of the following receptors is most likely responsible for this finding?
choices: B. Dopamine D2 in the nigrostriatal tract
C. Dopamine D2 in the tuberoinfundibular tract
questions.explanation: Orthostatic hypotension maps to α1-adrenergic blockade: α1 receptors mediate the reflex vasoconstriction that maintains blood pressure on standing, so blocking them → failure of that reflex → a symptomatic postural drop. Chlorpromazine is the prototypical low-potency typical, and the potency see-saw predicts this without knowing anything else about the molecule — low potency means low EPS but high anticholinergic, antihistaminic, and alpha-blocking burden. Board pearl — the receptor-to-side-effect map is worth memorizing as a five-line table: H1 gives sedation, α1 gives orthostatic hypotension, M1 gives dry mouth and blurred vision and urinary retention, nigrostriatal D2 gives EPS, and tuberoinfundibular D2 gives galactorrhea, amenorrhea, and gynecomastia.

wrongExplanations.1: Nigrostriatal D2 blockade tips the striatal acetylcholine:dopamine balance toward relative cholinergic excess and produces the extrapyramidal movement syndromes — dystonia, akathisia, pseudoparkinsonism, and tardive dyskinesia — not a postural blood pressure drop.
wrongExplanations.2: Tuberoinfundibular D2 blockade disinhibits prolactin release and produces galactorrhea, amenorrhea, and gynecomastia. It has no role in blood pressure regulation.
wrongExplanations.3: H1 antagonism produces sedation and contributes to weight gain. Chlorpromazine does block H1 heavily, which is why sedation is one of its signature effects, but sedation is not what makes blood pressure drop on standing.
wrongExplanations.4: M1 antagonism produces dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation, and urinary retention, and can cause tachycardia. It does not impair the vasoconstrictive reflex that fails here.

questions.eli5: When you stand up, your blood vessels are supposed to squeeze so blood keeps reaching your head. This medicine blocks the switch that tells them to squeeze, so his blood pressure drops and he gets dizzy every time he stands.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old man with schizophrenia has taken haloperidol for 4 months. His auditory hallucinations and his belief that his phone was reading his thoughts have resolved completely and have not returned. He now sits without spontaneous speech, answers questions in three-word phrases, shows almost no facial expression, and has stopped bathing or changing clothes unless prompted; his sister says he is noticeably more withdrawn than he was before the medication was started. He is afebrile, and examination shows no resting tremor, no cogwheel rigidity, no bradykinesia of the limbs, and no subjective urge to move. Which of the following best explains these findings?
choices: A. Insufficient D2 blockade in the mesolimbic tract at the current dose
B. D2 blockade in the already-hypodopaminergic mesocortical tract
C. D2 blockade in the nigrostriatal tract
D. D2 blockade in the tuberoinfundibular tract
E. 5-HT2A blockade in the mesolimbic tract
questions.explanation: Reason backward from the effect. Flat affect, alogia, avolition, and asociality are negative symptoms, and the mesocortical tract that governs cognition and motivation is already underactive in psychosis — so adding D2 blockade there worsens, or at best fails to help, exactly these symptoms. Haloperidol is a typical, meaning it blocks dopamine much more than serotonin and has essentially nothing extra to offer the mesocortical picture, which is why negative symptoms are described as untouched by typicals. Board pearl — atypicals, with their relatively greater 5-HT2A blockade, are historically the better option for negative symptoms and are the only agents that address cognitive symptoms at all, so this finding is an argument for changing class rather than raising the dose.

wrongExplanations.0: Insufficient mesolimbic blockade would present as persistent or returning positive symptoms — hallucinations and delusions. The stem states his hallucinations and delusions have resolved completely and have not returned.
wrongExplanations.2: Nigrostriatal blockade produces extrapyramidal findings, and drug-induced parkinsonism can genuinely masquerade as negative symptoms through masked facies and bradykinesia — which is why the stem explicitly excludes resting tremor, cogwheel rigidity, and limb bradykinesia.
wrongExplanations.3: Tuberoinfundibular blockade disinhibits prolactin and produces galactorrhea, amenorrhea, and gynecomastia. It has no relationship to affect, speech output, or motivation.
wrongExplanations.4: Haloperidol is a first-generation agent that blocks dopamine far more than serotonin, so meaningful 5-HT2A blockade is not part of its profile — and if anything, greater 5-HT2A blockade is associated with better rather than worse negative-symptom outcomes.

questions.eli5: The medicine turned down dopamine everywhere, including in the part of the brain that was already running too low. That is the part that supplies motivation, expression, and speech — so the voices stopped, but he went flat and quiet.

questions.stem: Information that would be most supportive of a secondary (organic) cause of a patient's new-onset psychosis rather than a primary psychotic disorder is that the patient:
choices: A. has a first-degree relative with schizophrenia.
B. smokes two packs of cigarettes daily.
C. has had two previous psychiatric hospitalizations for psychosis.
D. has had a marked decline in occupational functioning since the symptoms began.
questions.explanation: Prominent visual hallucinations are atypical for a primary psychotic disorder, in which auditory hallucinations dominate, so their presence should push the workup toward a secondary cause — substance-induced psychosis or psychosis due to a general medical condition. The other four options are all items from the list of history clues that favor a primary disorder, which is what makes them tempting: a family history of psychotic disorders, prior psychiatric hospitalization, prior antipsychotic treatment, marked postmorbid decline in function, and heavy smoking all argue for a psychiatric diagnosis rather than an organic one. Board pearl — a primary psychotic disorder is to some degree a diagnosis of exclusion, and an unremarkable physical examination is itself a useful pertinent negative supporting it.

wrongExplanations.0: A family history of psychotic disorders is one of the standard history clues favoring a primary psychotic disorder, since the heritable risk belongs to the psychiatric illness rather than to any organic cause.
wrongExplanations.1: Heavy smoking argues toward a primary disorder rather than away from it — roughly 95% of patients with psychotic disorders smoke cigarettes, which is why smoking status appears on the primary-disorder clue list.
wrongExplanations.2: Prior psychiatric hospitalizations for psychosis establish a recurrent psychiatric course, which is one of the strongest clues favoring a primary psychotic disorder.
wrongExplanations.3: Marked postmorbid decline in level of functioning is a listed feature of primary psychotic disorders, and it appears in the diagnostic criteria for schizophrenia itself.

questions.eli5: People with the psychiatric kind of psychosis usually hear things rather than see them. So when someone is mainly seeing things that are not there, doctors start looking for a medical cause instead — an infection, a drug, or something in the brain.

questions.stem: Raymond is a 47-year-old tax accountant who has been convinced for the past 3 years that the owner of the neighboring property is poisoning the soil along their shared fence line to force him to sell his house. He photographs the fence line every Saturday morning, has sent four certified letters, and has filed two complaints with the county, each of which was investigated and closed. He continues to work full-time and has filed every client return on schedule, has been married for 19 years, and golfs with the same three friends each weekend. He has never heard voices or seen anything others could not see, his speech is organized and goal-directed, his affect is full and reactive, and he shows no decline in self-care. He has never had a period of depressed or elevated mood. His wife describes him as "the most easygoing man in the world — until you mention that fence." The most likely diagnosis is
questions.explanation: Delusional disorder requires a plausible, non-bizarre fixed delusion with otherwise preserved functioning and no other prominent psychotic features — and a neighbor poisoning soil in a property dispute is entirely plausible, which is exactly what makes it non-bizarre. Everything outside the belief is intact: full-time work, a long marriage, a stable friend group, organized speech, reactive affect, and normal self-care. The wife's quote is the tiebreaker, because it establishes that the suspicion is encapsulated to one topic rather than a pervasive stance toward the world. Board pearl — the six delusion subtypes are persecutory, somatic, erotomanic, grandiose, jealous, and mixed, and the characteristic insight failure is limited to the delusion itself.

wrongExplanations.1: Paranoid personality disorder is a pervasive, lifelong pattern of distrust and suspiciousness across many relationships and situations, without a single fixed delusion. His wife's description places him at the opposite pole — easygoing about everything except this one belief.
wrongExplanations.2: Schizoaffective disorder requires major mood episodes concurrent with psychosis plus a period of at least 2 weeks of psychosis alone. He has never had a period of depressed or elevated mood at all.
wrongExplanations.3: Schizophrenia requires at least two of the core psychotic criteria along with decline in functioning. He has one symptom only, and his occupational, social, and self-care functioning are explicitly preserved across 3 years.
wrongExplanations.4: Schizotypal personality disorder involves odd beliefs and magical thinking, eccentric appearance and behavior, constricted affect, and social anxiety with few close relationships. His affect is full, his speech is organized, and he maintains a marriage and a regular social group.

questions.eli5: For three years he has believed one specific thing that could actually be true — that his neighbor is poisoning the dirt — and everything else about his life works fine. One fixed, believable false idea with normal functioning around it has its own name: delusional disorder.
